title: MEDI2004 W1 · Introduction to Pharmacology
subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
content: Drug = any substance producing a biological effect when administered (synthetic, natural, or genetically engineered). Endogenous substances aren't drugs unless administered (own insulin = hormone; injected = drug). Drug = active chemical; medicine = drug + excipients in a dose form (medicine contains the drug); drug class = drugs sharing mechanism/target/therapeutic use. Vitamins/herbs act as drugs when they produce effects (label doesn't decide). Pharmacology = study of drugs and their interactions with living systems; branches: pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, pharmacotherapeutics, toxicology, pharmacogenetics, clinical pharmacology. PK = body->drug (ADME; sets dose/timing); PD = drug->body (mechanism/effect; sets effect & side effects). Classes: analgesic (pain), anaesthetic (removes sensation), anxiolytic (anxiety), sedative (sleep), stimulant (CNS activity), antidepressant (SSRIs), antipsychotic, antihypertensive (ACE inhibitors), antineoplastic (cancer), anabolic steroid, hallucinogen, PrEP (HIV prevention). Prefixes: anti- = against, -lytic = relieves/breaks, an-/anaes- = without.

questions.question: Pharmacology is best defined as the study of:
options: A. how drugs and the body interact
B. how organs are surgically repaired
C. how diseases spread in populations
D. how cells divide during growth
questions.explanation: Pharmacology is the science of the interactions between drugs and living systems — spanning both what the drug does and what the body does to it.

questions.question: A drug is broadly defined as any substance that:
questions.explanation: A drug is a chemical that produces a biological effect by altering the function of a living system, rather than acting as a nutrient or building block.

questions.question: Morphine is an example of a drug originally obtained from:
questions.explanation: Morphine comes from the opium poppy — a plant source, one of the historic origins of drugs alongside microbes and synthesis.

questions.question: Pharmacokinetics describes what the:
options: A. body does to the drug
B. drug does to the body
C. doctor does to the patient
D. cell does to the gene
questions.explanation: Pharmacokinetics is body→drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion — how the body handles the drug over time.

questions.question: A student says a beta-blocker 'slows the heart by blocking β1 receptors.' This statement describes the drug's:
questions.explanation: Describing the mechanism by which a drug affects the body (receptor block → slower heart) is pharmacodynamics — drug→body.

questions.question: Saying 'the liver metabolises this drug within two hours' is a statement about its:
questions.explanation: Metabolism is one of the ADME processes, so describing how the body clears the drug is pharmacokinetics — body→drug.

questions.question: A tablet contains the active drug plus binders, coatings and fillers. The whole formulated product is best called a:
questions.explanation: A medicine is the active drug combined with excipients into a usable dose form; the drug is only the active ingredient within it.

questions.question: 'Paracetamol' is the generic name and 'Panadol' is one brand. The generic (non-proprietary) name is the one that is:
questions.explanation: The generic (INN) name is a single agreed name used internationally, whereas brand names are proprietary and vary by manufacturer.

questions.question: Every drug has three kinds of name. The one assigned by the WHO for use in all countries is the:
questions.explanation: The International Nonproprietary Name (generic name) is the globally recognised label; the chemical name describes structure and brand names are commercial.

questions.question: Penicillin, the first true antibiotic, was originally derived from a:
questions.explanation: Penicillin came from the Penicillium mould — a microbial source, illustrating drugs discovered from micro-organisms.

questions.question: Human insulin for injection is now made by genetically engineered bacteria, making it an example of a:
questions.explanation: Recombinant insulin is a protein produced by living cells — a biologic — rather than a chemically synthesised small molecule.

questions.question: Grouping drugs such as 'beta-blockers' or 'ACE inhibitors' organises them mainly by their:
questions.explanation: Drug classes are commonly defined by shared mechanism or target, which predicts their effects and typical uses.

questions.question: The branch of pharmacology concerned with the harmful effects of chemicals is:
questions.explanation: Toxicology studies the adverse and poisonous effects of substances, a specialised branch of pharmacology.

questions.question: Caffeine keeps you alert but has no nutritional role. By pharmacological definition caffeine is therefore a:
questions.explanation: Because it alters biological function (alertness) without providing nourishment, caffeine fits the definition of a drug.

questions.question: Clinical pharmacology is distinguished from basic pharmacology mainly by its focus on:
questions.explanation: Clinical pharmacology applies drug science to real patients — dosing, safety and effectiveness — rather than purely laboratory mechanisms.

questions.question: Before a new drug is tested in humans, it must first pass through:
questions.explanation: Preclinical (lab and animal) studies assess basic safety and activity before any first-in-human clinical trial can begin.

questions.question: The four processes summarised by the abbreviation ADME are absorption, distribution, metabolism and:
questions.explanation: ADME stands for Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism and Excretion — the four stages of a drug's journey through the body.

questions.question: Two statements are made about a drug: it 'binds µ-opioid receptors' and it 'is cleared by the kidney.' These describe, in order:
questions.explanation: Receptor binding is the drug's action on the body (PD); renal clearance is the body's handling of the drug (PK).

questions.question: A name like 'N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetamide' for paracetamol is which type of drug name?
questions.explanation: The chemical name describes the molecule's structure; it is distinct from the shorter generic name and the commercial brand name.

questions.question: Two brands of ibuprofen contain identical active drug but different fillers and coatings. What differs between them is the:
questions.explanation: The active drug is the same; the products differ only as medicines — in their excipients and formulation, not their pharmacology.

questions.question: Two drugs share a mechanism but treat different conditions. Classifying them together by mechanism is useful mainly because it predicts their:
questions.explanation: A shared mechanism implies shared pharmacological effects and a similar side-effect profile, which is why mechanism-based classes are clinically handy.

questions.question: The study of how inherited genetic differences change a patient's response to drugs is called:
questions.explanation: Pharmacogenomics links genetic variation to drug response; pharmacognosy studies natural drug sources and pharmacovigilance monitors safety.

questions.question: Pharmacognosy, one of the older branches, is specifically the study of drugs derived from:
questions.explanation: Pharmacognosy deals with medicines obtained from plants and other natural sources — the traditional starting point of drug discovery.

questions.question: The branch of pharmacology that monitors a medicine's safety after it is marketed is:
questions.explanation: Pharmacovigilance is post-marketing surveillance — detecting and evaluating adverse effects once the drug is in wide use.

questions.question: Why does understanding pharmacokinetics matter for choosing a dosing interval? Because it predicts how fast the drug is:
questions.explanation: Dosing frequency depends on how quickly the body eliminates the drug; that clearance rate is exactly what pharmacokinetics quantifies.

questions.question: A poison and a therapeutic drug can be the same substance, differing chiefly in the:
questions.explanation: As Paracelsus noted, the dose makes the poison — the same chemical can heal or harm depending on how much is given.
